newsitem.title: UK: Major fires starting gun for bitter leadership scrap.
newsitem.headline: Major fires starting gun for bitter leadership scrap.

text.p: John Major's decision to step down as leader of the British Conservative Party looks certain to set off a bitter battle for his succession, with the running sore of policy towards Europe which beset his premiership at the centre of the scrap.

Major said as he left his Downing Street office for the last time on Friday following the opposition Labour Party's landslide election win: "When the curtain falls, it is time to get off the stage. That is what I propose to do."
Following his announcement, politicians and analysts speculated on how much more damage the contest that must now ensue will do to a party which has already taken a huge battering from the voters.

"The civil war...will now break out in earnest, and I think it will disable the Conservative Party for some time to come," Paddy Ashdown, the triumphant leader of the minority Liberal Democrats, who have made big gains, told BBC television.

The scale of the Conservative defeat -- they look like having just a quarter of Britain's 659 members of parliament instead of half -- and Major's apparent decision to go quickly, mean that some potential successors are out of the running.
Michael Portillo, who had been Major's Defence Secretary, and is the darling of the Eurosceptic right, was defeated in his north London constituency.
His Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind perished in the debacle in Scotland, where the Conservatives lost every seat they had held.

And Chris Patten, once spoken of as a possible eventual successor to Major, cannot return to British politics until the end of next month, when his job as Britain's last governor of Hong Kong ends when the colony reverts to Chinese rule.
This leaves outgoing Welsh Secretary William Hague, a youthful 36, and Michael Heseltine, 64, who was Major's deputy Prime Minister, as two likely contenders.

Bookmakers William Hill made the two men favourites, with the moderately pro-Europe Heseltine at 7/4 to become what would be surely be, given his age, a stopgap leader, followed by the more Eurosceptical Hague at 2/1.

Both men appeared at Conservative headquarters as the first election results came in to urge "a period of reflection" before any decisions about the party's future direction were taken. But now Major has decided to quit, that will be impossible.
Portillo's enforced absence could be a big boost for John Redwood, the former cabinet minister who challenged Major for the party leadership two years ago.
Portillo and Redwood, 45, were until Thursday regarded as the two potential challengers from the Eurosceptic right.

The much-reduced band of less than 170 Conservative MPs will be the only ones with the right to vote in the election. If they are worried that Redwood would be incapable of uniting the party, and might even provoke resignations from senior figures, they could go for a compromise candidate.
Names that have been canvassed include former interior minister Michael Howard, a rightwinger, and outgoing health secretary Stephen Dorrell.

But the chances of outgoing finance minister Kenneth Clarke - the first declared candidate - look slim as many Conservatives are hostile to his sympathetic stance toward Brussels. William Hill made him 8/1, longer odds than for both Redwood and Howard.
